lines.title: Here's one sample site for the College-Town Home Sales case. It isn't the answer key, and it isn't the only way to build it.
lines.first-look: The whole site is one long page. Ten questions come first, then a section to explore the data, two short insights, and the data and methods.
lines.questions-intro: Questions one to six always use the full dataset. Seven to ten change with the visitor's own settings.
lines.q1: Question one asks which city has the highest median sale price. The site writes the answer out, Davis, California, at eight hundred eighty-nine thousand dollars, and then shows it in a bar chart.
lines.q2: Question two compares each city's mean and median price. Athens, Georgia has the widest gap, thirty-two point eight percent, and the site explains what causes it.
lines.q3: For question three, a slope chart shows which cities change rank once the price rule is applied.
lines.q4: Question four uses a bar chart for the change in median price from 2024 to 2025.
lines.q5: Question five uses a box plot, so you see the spread of days on market, not only the median.
lines.q6: And question six compares the property tax burden with a dot chart.
lines.q7: From question seven on, the visitor picks the settings. Change the number of bedrooms, and the answer and the chart update.
lines.q8: Question eight takes any price range you type in.
lines.q9: Question nine counts the sales in each month, for a city and year you choose.
lines.q10: And question ten finds how far from campus the homes are, for a campus area, a budget and a number of bedrooms.
lines.insights: The insights section has two short notes. One on data quality, and one on what it was like to work with a coding agent.
lines.feature-01: Filters for place, year, bedrooms and price, with key numbers that update as you change them.
lines.feature-02: A map of the campus areas. Click one, and the whole section filters to it.
lines.feature-03: A range filter you can drag, or type into. The slider and the number boxes stay in sync.
lines.feature-04: Filters for garage, basement and fireplace, where a blank counts as unknown, not as no.
lines.feature-05: Shareable filters. The settings live in the page address, so opening a copied link brings back the same view.
lines.feature-06: A side-by-side comparison of any two places.
lines.feature-07: A table that sorts when you click a column heading, with icons that show the column and the direction.
lines.feature-08: A layout that works on a desktop and on a phone, with no sideways scrolling.
lines.feature-09: A light and a dark mode, where the charts, the map and the controls follow the theme.
lines.feature-10: And a data and methods section with the rules behind every number. Across the ten questions, the site uses seven chart types.
lines.design: Finally, the design. A serif for headings and a sans serif for text. A small color palette, with the answer in the accent color. Even spacing, styled controls, finished charts, and small touches like a loading message and a real page title.
lines.closing: Your site will look different, and that's expected. Check your numbers against the rules in the case, not against this video.
